content: If tuberculosis (TB) disease develops, treatment should be initiated with an appropriate drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) regimen based on the drug susceptibility testing (DST) pattern of the presumed source case. It is important for healthcare providers to recognize that younger children are at a higher risk of progressing to active TB disease. The treatment of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) in children follows the same principles and utilizes the same second-line drugs as in adults. However, the optimal duration of these regimens in children remains unknown. MDR-TB in children is associated with poorer treatment outcomes and higher mortality rates compared to drug-sensitive TB. For cases of monoresistant TB, where resistance to isoniazid is known or suspected, or in areas with high prevalence of isoniazid resistance, the addition of ethambutol to isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide during the intensive phase is recommended. In patients with more extensive disease, the inclusion of a fluoroquinolone and extending treatment to a minimum of nine months should be considered. Monoresistance to rifampicin should be treated with isoniazid, ethambutol, and a fluoroquinolone for at least 12–18 months, with pyrazinamide added for the first two months. Polyresistant TB, defined as resistance to two or more first-line drugs but not both isoniazid and rifampicin, requires tailored treatment regimens. Suggested regimens are available for such cases. Children with MDR-TB are treated similarly to adults with MDR-TB. However, in children, confirmation of the diagnosis and DST may not always be feasible, necessitating empirical treatment based on the likely source case. Although data on treatment outcomes in children are limited, available evidence suggests that outcomes comparable to those in adults can be achieved. Management should adhere to the following principles: Never add a single drug to a failing regimen, as this may lead to amplification of resistance. Administer all treatment daily under direct observation. Base treatment on DST results from the likely source case unless DST results are available from the child. Perform second-line DST in all MDR-TB cases to exclude resistance to fluoroquinolones and/or second-line injectables, as this may necessitate additional drugs early in therapy. Use at least three, preferably four, drugs to which the patient or source case is naïve or the isolate is susceptible. Provide counseling and support to caregivers at every follow-up visit regarding adverse effects, treatment duration, and the importance of adherence. Adjust drug dosages to account for weight gain in children. Monitor clinical, radiographic, and culture responses to treatment. Monthly smear microscopy and cultures should be performed until three consecutive negative results are obtained, after which follow-up cultures can be done every 2–3 months. Conduct clinical monitoring for adverse effects at every visit, guided by the adverse effect profile of the drugs used. While any of the drugs described for MDR-TB treatment may be used in children, safety data in children currently exist only for fluoroquinolones. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for MDR-TB treatment in children address the use of fluoroquinolones specifically. There is a need for safety data on other drugs used in treating children with MDR-TB. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by MDR bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone as part of a well-functioning MDR-TB control program and within an appropriate MDR-TB regimen. The decision to treat should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. Building a treatment regimen for MDR-TB in children follows the same principles as in adults. For extensive pulmonary or disseminated extrapulmonary disease, a minimum of four to six drugs should be included in the regimen, based on the susceptibilities of the isolate. The progression of drug selection includes: 1. Use any Group 1 first-line oral drugs with known or likely efficacy, based on DST results. 2. Add one Group 2 injectable agent, typically an aminoglycoside like amikacin, for a minimum of six months and four months after culture conversion. Streptomycin is not recommended due to high resistance rates and ototoxicity. 3. Add one Group 3 fluoroquinolone, such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, for the duration of therapy. Ciprofloxacin is not recommended. 4. Add Group 4 second-line oral drugs until at least four effective drugs are included in the regimen. Drug selection should consider treatment history, adverse effect profiles, and cost. 5. If a regimen of four effective drugs cannot be built from Groups 1–4, consider adding at least two Group 5 third-line drugs in consultation with an MDR-TB expert. Optimal dosing of second-line drugs in children is not well established, and pediatric formulations are often unavailable. Tablets may need to be broken or cut, leading to potential inaccuracies in dosing. The taste of medications is often unpalatable, and some drugs can cause vomiting and diarrhea, affecting drug absorption. Daily injectable drugs are typically given during the initial months of treatment, and the pill burden can be substantial. Splitting the daily dose or mixing drugs with food or drinks may improve tolerability but complicates directly observed therapy (DOT). The duration of treatment for MDR-TB in children depends on the extent of the disease. The intensive phase typically lasts at least eight months, with a total treatment duration of at least 10 months. All treatment should be administered daily under direct observation. The optimal duration of treatment for MDR-TB in children is unknown, and further research is needed. Adverse effects occur less frequently in children than in adults. However, the risks and benefits of each drug should be carefully considered when designing a regimen. Caregivers should be informed about potential adverse events and instructed to report them immediately. No second-line anti-TB drugs are absolutely contraindicated in children, and they should not be withheld unless hypersensitivity or intractable adverse reactions are documented. Regular monitoring of body weight is essential to adjust drug dosages as the child grows. Baseline audiometry and monthly hearing tests are mandatory if Group 2 injectable agents are used, particularly aminoglycosides, due to the risk of ototoxicity. This is especially important in high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes, HIV, or renal insufficiency. Additional management considerations for DR-TB in children include: HIV-positive children with DR-TB should receive pyridoxine, cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), and antiretroviral therapy (ART), which significantly improves treatment outcomes. Corticosteroids may be used as indicated for drug-susceptible TB and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Nutritional support is crucial for children with DR-TB. Infection control measures are essential to prevent the spread of DR-TB. Adherence to treatment is critical to prevent further development of resistance. Adverse effects associated with firstand second-line drugs used in children with MDRand XDR-TB should be closely monitored. For example, isoniazid may cause hepatotoxicity, rash, or peripheral neuropathy, while pyrazinamide can lead to hepatotoxicity or arthralgia. Ethambutol carries a risk of optic neuritis, and injectable agents like amikacin may cause ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity. Fluoroquinolones can result in gastrointestinal disturbances or insomnia. Group 4 drugs, such as ethionamide, may cause gastrointestinal upset or hepatotoxicity, while cycloserine can lead to psychosis or depression. Group 5 drugs, like linezolid, may cause myelosuppression or lactic acidosis. Adherence to both anti-TB treatment and ART is critical. The unpleasant taste of some drugs, nausea, vomiting, and the high pill burden can complicate adherence. If home treatment is not feasible, daily injectables should be administered at a local health clinic, and hospitalization may be necessary in some cases. Children should be monitored to assess response to therapy, identify adverse events early, and promote adherence.
